events.title: Elixir 1.0 released
events.summary: José Valim released Elixir 1.0 on September 18, 2015 — the first stable version on the Erlang BEAM VM with macros, protocols, and Mix tooling.
events.about: Elixir 1.0 committed to stability for production: Phoenix web framework, OTP supervision trees, and pipelines for data transformation. Discord, Pinterest, and Bleacher Report adopted it for real-time, fault-tolerant backends.

narrative.whyChosen: Elixir 1.0 was the milestone that let teams ship BEAM-based systems beyond experiments.
narrative.whyImportant: Stable tooling and semantics unlocked Elixir for production web and telecom workloads.
narrative.problemSolved: Pre-1.0 Elixir changed too fast for companies to standardize on it.

events.title: Phoenix 1.0 released
events.summary: Chris McCord released Phoenix 1.0 on September 12, 2015 — a productive Elixir web framework with channels for real-time WebSocket apps.
events.about: Phoenix brought Rails-like productivity to Elixir: generators, Ecto for databases, and channels for live updates. It powered Discord-scale chat, dashboards, and APIs where BEAM fault tolerance mattered — proving Elixir was more than a syntax experiment.

narrative.whyChosen: Phoenix 1.0 was the web framework that made Elixir production-credible.
narrative.whyImportant: Channels and OTP supervision brought real-time features without fragile Node clusters.
narrative.problemSolved: Elixir needed a batteries-included web stack to compete with Rails and Django.

events.title: Node.js 4.0 released
events.summary: Node.js 4.0.0 shipped on September 8, 2015 — merging the io.js fork back into Node with V8 4.5, native ES6 support, and an LTS schedule.
events.about: Node 4 ended the io.js schism and established even-numbered LTS releases. Arrow functions, classes, and template literals worked natively; npm 2 shipped bundled. It became the baseline for Express, Koa, and the MEAN/MERN stacks of the mid-2010s.

narrative.whyChosen: Node 4 reunited the community after the io.js fork and defined modern Node LTS.
narrative.whyImportant: The LTS policy gave enterprises a stable line while odd versions experimented.
narrative.problemSolved: The io.js fork split contributors and left production teams unsure which runtime to ship.

events.title: Safari 9 released
events.summary: Apple released Safari 9 on September 30, 2015 with OS X El Capitan — adding pinned tabs, AirPlay support, and improved JavaScript performance.
events.about: Safari 9 refined the El Capitan experience with muteable tabs, content blocking extensions, and CSS scroll snapping. It kept WebKit competitive as mobile browsing overtook desktop for many sites.

narrative.whyChosen: Safari 9 added content blockers and pinned tabs that shaped desktop browsing habits.
narrative.whyImportant: Content blocking extensions changed the ad and privacy landscape on Mac.
narrative.problemSolved: Users wanted Safari-native ad blocking without third-party plugins like Flash.
